Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this paper, we are concerned with two SIS epidemic reaction-diffusion models with mass action infection mechanism of the form S​ISI, and study the spatial profile of population distribution as the movement rate of the infected individuals is restricted to be small. For the model with a constant total population number, our results show that the susceptible population always converges to a positive constant which is indeed the minimum of the associated risk function, and the infected population either concentrates at the isolated highest-risk points or aggregates only on the highest-risk intervals once the highest-risk locations contain at least one interval. In sharp contrast, for the model with a varying total population number which is caused by the recruitment of the susceptible individuals and death of the infected individuals, our results reveal that the susceptible population converges to a positive function which is non-constant unless the associated risk function is constant, and the infected population may concentrate only at some isolated highest-risk points, or aggregate at least in a neighborhood of the highest-risk locations or occupy the whole habitat, depending on the behavior of the associated risk function and even its smoothness at the highest-risk locations. Numerical simulations are performed to support and complement our theoretical findings.

Key words and phrases: 
Reaction-diffusion SIS epidemic model; mass action infection mechanism; spatial profile; small movement rate; heterogeneous environment.

1. Introduction and existing results

The outbreak of the novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) continues to spread rapidly around the world, and it has caused tremendous impacts on public health and the global economy. As it is commonly recognized, population movement is a significant factor in the spread of many reported infectious diseases including COVID-19 [5, 9, 25], and the lockdown and quarantine has turned out to be one of the most effective measures to reduce or even eliminate the infection [30, 60]. On the other hand, the importance of the population heterogeneity has also been observed in the complicated dynamical behaviour of the transmission of COVID-19 [7, 8, 17].

To gain a deeper understanding of the impact of population movement and heterogeneity on the transmission of epidemic diseases from a mathematically theoretical viewpoint, in the present work we are concerned with two SIS reaction-diffusion systems with mass action infection mechanism in a heterogeneous environment. We aim to study the spatial profile of population distribution as the movement rate of the infected individuals is controlled to be sufficiently small. Such kind of information may be useful for decision-makers to predict the pattern of disease occurrence and henceforth to conduct more effective strategies of disease eradication. The mass action infection mechanism was first proposed in the seminal work of Kermack and McKendrick [26], in which the disease transmission was assumed to be governed by a bilinear incidence function S​ISI (one may also refer to [27, 28, 29] or [54]). The systems under consideration in this paper are possibly the simplest yet basic SIS epidemic models.

The first model we will deal with in this work is the following coupled reaction-diffusion equations in one-dimensional space:

{St−dSSx​x=−β(x)SI+γ(x)I,0<x<L,t>0,It−dIIx​x=β(x)SI−γ(x)I,0<x<L,t>0,Sx=Ix=0,x=0,L,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x)≥0,I(x,0)=I0(x)≥,≢0,0<x<L.\begin{cases}S_{t}-d_{S}S_{xx}=-\beta(x)SI+\gamma(x)I,\ \ \ &0<x<L,\ \ t>0,\\ I_{t}-d_{I}I_{xx}=\beta(x)SI-\gamma(x)I,\ \ \ &0<x<L,\ \ t>0,\\ S_{x}=I_{x}=0,\ \ \ &x=0,\,L,\ \ t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ I(x,0)=I_{0}(x)\geq,\not\equiv 0,\ &0<x<L.\end{cases} (1.1)

Here, S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) and I⁡(x,t)I(x,t) are respectively the population density of the susceptible and infected individuals at position x∈[0,L]x\in[0,L] and time tt; the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition means that no population flux crosses the boundary x=0,Lx=0,\,L; dSd_{S} and dId_{I} are positive constants measuring the motility of susceptible and infected individuals, respectively; and the functions β\beta and γ\gamma are Hölder continuous positive functions in [0,L][0,L] representing the disease transmission rate and the disease recovery rate, respectively.

Integrating the sum of the equations of (1.1), combined with the homogeneous Neumann boundary value conditions, we observe that

∫0L(S⁡(x,t)+I⁡(x,t))​𝑑x=∫0L(S0​(x)+I0​(x))​𝑑x=:N,∀t≥0.\int^{L}_{0}(S(x,t)+I(x,t))\,{\rm d}x=\int^{L}_{0}(S_{0}(x)+I_{0}(x))\,{\rm d}x=:N,\ \ \ \forall t\geq 0.

Thus, the total population number in (1.1) is conserved all the time.

The system (1.1) was investigated in the recent works [16, 68, 65]; in particular, when the movement of either the susceptible or infected population is restricted to be slow, the authors explored the profile of the spatial distribution of the disease modelled by (1.1). The understanding of such a profile amounts to determine the behavior of the so-called endemic equilibrium with respect to the small diffusion rate dSd_{S} or dId_{I}. The endemic equilibrium of (1.1) is a positive steady state solution, which satisfies the following elliptic system:

{−dSSx​x=−β(x)SI+γ(x)I,0<x<L,−dIIx​x=β(x)SI−γ(x)I,0<x<L,Sx=Ix=0,x=0,L,∫0L(S⁡(x)+I⁡(x))​dx=N.\begin{cases}-d_{S}S_{xx}=-\beta(x)SI+\gamma(x)I,\ \ \ &0<x<L,\\ -d_{I}I_{xx}=\beta(x)SI-\gamma(x)I,\ \ \ &0<x<L,\\ S_{x}=I_{x}=0,\ \ \ &x=0,L,\\ \displaystyle\int^{L}_{0}(S(x)+I(x))\,{\rm d}x=N.\end{cases} (1.2)

According to [16, 68, 65], if minx∈[0,L]⁡γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)<NL\min_{x\in[0,L]}\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)}<\frac{N}{L}, for any small dI>0d_{I}>0, (1.2) admits at least one positive solution (S,I)(S,I), which is called an endemic equilibrium (EE for abbreviation) in terms of epidemiology; moreover, (S,I)(S,I) satisfies S,I∈C2​([0,L])S,\,I\in C^{2}([0,L]) and S,I>0S,\,I>0 on [0,L][0,L].

As remarked in [68], it is a challenging problem to study the spatial profile of EE of (1.2) with respect to the small movement rate dId_{I} of the infected population; in [65], the authors provided a first result in this research direction. Indeed, they proved the following conclusion.

Theorem 1.1.

[65, Theorem B] Assume that minx∈[0,L]⁡γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)<NL\min_{x\in[0,L]}\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)}<\frac{N}{L}. Then as dI→0d_{I}\rightarrow 0, the EE (S,I)(S,I) of (1.2) satisfies (up to a sequence of dId_{I}) that S→S^S\to\hat{S} uniformly on [0,L][0,L], where S^∈C⁡([0,L])\hat{S}\in C([0,L]) with min[0,L]⁡γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)≤S^​(x)≤max[0,L]⁡γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)\min_{[0,L]}\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)}\leq\hat{S}(x)\leq\max_{[0,L]}\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)}, and I→μI\to\mu weakly for some Radon measure μ\mu with nonempty support in the sense of

∫0LI⁡(x)​ζ​(x)​𝑑x⟶∫[0,L]ζ⁡(x)​μ​(𝑑x),∀ζ∈C⁡([0,L]).\displaystyle\int_{0}^{L}I(x)\zeta(x){\rm d}x\longrightarrow\int_{[0,L]}\zeta(x)\mu({\rm d}x),\ \ \ \forall\zeta\in C([0,L]). (1.3)

Obviously, Theorem 1.1 does not give a precise description for S^\hat{S} and μ\mu and hence the spatial profile of the susceptible and infected populations remains obscure. From the aspect of disease control, it becomes imperative to know an informative behavior of μ\mu. In this paper, we manage to give a satisfactory result on the profile of S^\hat{S} and μ\mu.

In (1.1), some important factors such as the death and recruitment rates of population are ignored so that the total population number is a constant. In order to take into account the death and recruitment rates of population, the following reaction-diffusion epidemic system was proposed in [40]:

{St−dS​Sx​x=Λ⁡(x)−S−β⁡(x)​S​I+γ⁡(x)​I,0<x​<L,t>​0,It−dI​Ix​x=β⁡(x)​S​I−[γ⁡(x)+η⁡(x)]​I,0<x​<L,t>​0,Sx=Ix=0,x=0,L,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x)≥0,I(x,0)=I0(x)≥,≢0,0<x<L.\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}S_{t}-d_{S}S_{xx}=\Lambda(x)-S-\beta(x)SI+\gamma(x)I,&0<x<L,\,t>0,\\ I_{t}-d_{I}I_{xx}=\beta(x)SI-\left[\gamma(x)+\eta(x)\right]I,&0<x<L,\,t>0,\\ S_{x}=I_{x}=0,&x=0,L,\,t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x)\geq 0,\,I(x,0)=I_{0}(x)\geq,\not\equiv 0,&0<x<L.\end{array}\right. (1.4)

The recruitment term of the susceptible population is represented by the function Λ⁡(x)−S\Lambda(x)-S so that the susceptible is subject to the linear growth/death ([4, 24]); η⁡(x)\eta(x) accounts for the death rate of the infected. Here, Λ,η\Lambda,\,\eta are assumed to be positive Hölder continuous functions on [0,L][0,L]. All other parameters have the same interpretation as in (1.1).

It is easily seen that the following elliptic problem

−dS​Sx​x=Λ⁡(x)−S, 0<x<L;Sx​(0)=Sx​(L)=0\displaystyle-d_{S}S_{xx}=\Lambda(x)-S,\ \ 0<x<L;\ \ \ S_{x}(0)=S_{x}(L)=0 (1.5)

admits a unique positive solution S~\tilde{S}. Then (S~,0)(\tilde{S},0) is a unique disease-free equilibrium of (1.4). An EE of (1.4) satisfies the following ODE system:

{−dSSx​x=Λ(x)−S−β(x)SI+γ(x)I,0<x<L,−dIIx​x=β(x)SI−[γ(x)+η(x)]I,0<x<L,Sx=Ix=0,x=0,L.\begin{cases}-d_{S}S_{xx}=\Lambda(x)-S-\beta(x)SI+\gamma(x)I,\ \ \ &0<x<L,\\ -d_{I}I_{xx}=\beta(x)SI-\left[\gamma(x)+\eta(x)\right]I,\ \ \ &0<x<L,\\ S_{x}=I_{x}=0,\ \ \ &x=0,L.\end{cases} (1.6)

As one of the main results of [40], the following conclusion on the profile of EE of (1.6) with respect to small dId_{I} was established.

Theorem 1.2.

[40, Theorem 3.2] Assume that the set {x∈[0,L]:β⁡(x)​S~​(x)>γ⁡(x)+η⁡(x)}\{x\in[0,L]:\ \beta(x)\tilde{S}(x)>\gamma(x)+\eta(x)\} is non-empty. As dI→0d_{I}\rightarrow 0, then any EE (S,I)\left(S,I\right) of (1.6) satisfies (up to a subsequence of dId_{I}) that S→S^uniformly on​[0,L],S\to\hat{S}\ \ \mbox{uniformly on}\ [0,L], where S^∈C⁡([0,L])\hat{S}\in C([0,L]) and S^>0\hat{S}>0 on [0,L][0,L], and ∫0LI​𝑑x→I^\int_{0}^{L}I{\rm d}x\to\hat{I} for some positive constant I^\hat{I}.

As in Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.2 does not characterize the precise distribution of the susceptible and infected populations. In this paper, we will also provide a clear picture of the population distributions for (1.6) as the movement rate dId_{I} tends to zero. It turns out that the spatial profiles of the disease distribution modelled by (1.2) and (1.6) are rather different.

The rest of paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we state the main theoretical results, and section 3 is devoted to their proofs. In section 4, we carry out the numerical simulations and discuss the implications of our results in terms of disease control. In the appendix, we recall some known facts which will be used in the paper.

2. Statement of main results

In this section, we state the main findings of this paper on models (1.2) and (1.6). To proceed, we underline some terminologies frequently used throughout the paper. For model (1.2), we call γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)} the risk function, and call each element of the set {x∈[0,L]:γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)=minx∈[0,L]⁡γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)}\big\{x\in[0,L]:\ \frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)}=\min_{x\in[0,L]}\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)}\big\} the highest-risk point (or location). Similarly, for model (1.6), we call γ⁡(x)+η⁡(x)β⁡(x)\frac{\gamma(x)+\eta(x)}{\beta(x)} the risk function, and call each element of the set {x∈[0,L]:γ⁡(x)+η⁡(x)β⁡(x)=minx∈[0,L]⁡γ⁡(x)+η⁡(x)β⁡(x)}\big\{x\in[0,L]:\ \frac{\gamma(x)+\eta(x)}{\beta(x)}=\min_{x\in[0,L]}\frac{\gamma(x)+\eta(x)}{\beta(x)}\big\} the highest-risk point (or location).

2.1. Results for model (1.2)

For the sake of convenience, we set

k⁡(x)=γ⁡(x)β⁡(x),km​i​n=minx∈[0,L]⁡k⁡(x),k(x)=\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)},\ \ \ \ k_{min}=\min_{x\in[0,L]}k(x),

and

Θk={x∈[0,L]:k⁡(x)=km​i​n}.\Theta_{k}=\big\{x\in[0,L]:\ k(x)=k_{min}\big\}.

We note that when the risk function k⁡(x)=kk(x)=k is a positive constant, it follows from [65] that S⁡(x)≡kS(x)\equiv k is a constant, and in turn by the equation of II, we immediately see that I=NL−kI=\frac{N}{L}-k is also a positive constant provided that k<NLk<\frac{N}{L}. Assume that k⁡(x)k(x) is non-constant and km​i​n<NLk_{min}<\frac{N}{L}. Then as dI→0d_{I}\rightarrow 0, the EE (S,I)(S,I) of (1.2) satisfies

S⁡(x)→km​i​nuniformly for​x∈[0,L].\displaystyle S(x)\to k_{min}\ \ \ \mbox{uniformly for}\ x\in[0,L]. (2.7)

The following assertions hold for the asymptotic behavior of II.

Regarding Theorem 2.1, we would like to make some comments in order as follows.

Remark 2.1.

In addition to the two cases treated in Theorem 2.1, we can handle some more general cases. In particular, we would like to make the following comments.

Nevertheless, we can not determine the exact values of cic_{i}; in other words, as dI→0d_{I}\to 0, it is unclear to us whether II concentrates at all xi​(1≤i≤j)x_{i}\ (1\leq i\leq j) or only some of them. The numerical results suggest that the former alternative holds; see Figure 1 in section 4.

    If the set Θk\Theta_{k} contains at least one proper interval of [0,L][0,L], by adapting the argument of Theorem 2.1(ii), we can show that S→km​i​nS\to k_{min} uniformly on [0,L][0,L], and I→I^I\to\hat{I} uniformly on [0,L][0,L] with

    and in (ϱ¯i,ϱ¯i)​(1≤i≤j∗)(\underline{\varrho}_{i},\,\overline{\varrho}_{i})\ (1\leq i\leq j_{*}), either I^=0\hat{I}=0 or I^>0\hat{I}>0. Without loss of generality, assuming that I^​(x)>0\hat{I}(x)>0 for x∈⋃i=1j∗^(ϱ¯i,ϱ¯i)x\in\bigcup_{i=1}^{\hat{j_{*}}}(\underline{\varrho}_{i},\,\overline{\varrho}_{i}) for some 1≤j∗^≤j∗1\leq\hat{j_{*}}\leq j_{*}, then in each such (ϱ¯i,ϱ¯i)(\underline{\varrho}_{i},\,\overline{\varrho}_{i}), we can conclude that I^\hat{I} solves

    {−I^x​x=β⁡(x)dS(a^−I^)I^,ϱ¯i<x<ϱ¯i,I^=0,x=ϱ¯i,ϱ¯i,\begin{cases}-\hat{I}_{xx}=\frac{\beta(x)}{d_{S}}(\hat{a}-\hat{I})\hat{I},\ \ &\underline{\varrho}_{i}<x<\overline{\varrho}_{i},\\ \hat{I}=0,\ \ &x=\underline{\varrho}_{i},\,\overline{\varrho}_{i},\end{cases}

    However, it seems rather challenging to prove whether I^\hat{I} is positive on all intervals (ϱ¯i,ϱ¯i)​(1≤i≤j∗)(\underline{\varrho}_{i},\,\overline{\varrho}_{i})\ (1\leq i\leq j_{*}) or only on some of them. Our numerical results suggest that the former alternative holds; see Figure 2 in section 4.

  • (iii)

    The assertion in (ii) above suggests that if the highest-risk locations contain at least one interval, then the disease can not stay on any possible isolated highest-risk points once the infected individuals move slowly.

Remark 2.2.

In the case (ii) of Theorem 2.1, if ϱ1=0\varrho_{1}=0 (or ϱ2=L\varrho_{2}=L), the results of Theorem 2.1 still hold true if we replace the Dirichlet boundary condition of I^\hat{I} in (2.8) at ϱ1=0\varrho_{1}=0 (or ϱ2=L\varrho_{2}=L) by the Neumann boundary condition I^x​(0)=0\hat{I}_{x}(0)=0 (or I^x​(L)=0\hat{I}_{x}(L)=0). A similar remark applies to the case discussed in Remark 2.1(ii) above.

Remark 2.3.

After this paper was finished, we noticed the work [10] in which the authors derived (2.7) and the convergence of the II-component in the case (i) of Theorem 2.1 in any spatial dimension in a more general setting; see Theorem 2.5(i) there. However, their result does not establish the convergence of the II-component within Θk\Theta_{k} in the case (ii) of Theorem 2.1 nor in the more general case mentioned by Remark 2.1; on the other hand, our proof of (2.7) and the convergence of the II-component outside of Θk\Theta_{k} is rather different from that of [10].

2.2. Results for model (1.6)

We now turn to system (1.6). For the sake of simplicity, we assume that Λ\Lambda in (1.6) is a positive constant, and also denote

h⁡(x)=γ⁡(x)+η⁡(x)β⁡(x),hm​i​n=minx∈[0,L]⁡h⁡(x),h(x)=\frac{\gamma(x)+\eta(x)}{\beta(x)},\ \ \ \ h_{min}=\min_{x\in[0,L]}h(x),

Λ>h⁡(x)for allx∈[0,L].\displaystyle\Lambda>h(x)\ \ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ x\in[0,L]. (2.9)

Now we can state our main findings on the asymptotic behavior of any EE (S,I)(S,I) of (1.6) as dI→0d_{I}\rightarrow 0. The first result reads as follows.

Theorem 2.2.

For model (1.2), our result shows that the infected population concentrates or aggregates only at the highest-risk locations. In sharp contrast, for model (1.6), our result suggests that the disease will occupy a neighborhood of the interior highest-risk locations or even occupy the whole habitat [0,L][0,L], or concentrates only at the boundary highest-risk location, depending on the risk function hh. More detailed discussions on the implications of our theoretical results, along with numerical simulations, will be given in section 4.

We would like to make some remarks on Theorem 2.3 as follows.

It is worth mentioning that all the statements in Theorem 2.3 except the expression (2.19) for the Radon measure μ\mu remain true provided that the risk function h∈C1​([0,L])h\in C^{1}([0,L]). Such a comment also applies to Lemmas 3.1-3.4 in the forthcoming section.

  4. (iv)

3. Proof of main results: Theorems 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorems 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3.

3.1. Proof of Theorem 2.1

In this subsection, we present the proof of Theorem 2.1.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

3.3. Proof of Theorem 2.3

This subsection is devoted to the proof of Theorem 2.3. We begin with some lemmas as follows.

S^​(ϱ0)=h⁡(ϱ0)=hm​i​nandS^<h in (ϱ0−ϵ1,ϱ0+ϵ1)∖{ϱ0}\hat{S}(\varrho_{0})=h(\varrho_{0})=h_{min}\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \hat{S}<h\ \ \mbox{ in $(\varrho_{0}-\epsilon_{1},\varrho_{0}+\epsilon_{1})\setminus\{\varrho_{0}\}$}

for some small ϵ1>0\epsilon_{1}>0.

Note that μ⁡([0,L])<∞\mu([0,L])<\infty. In view of this fact, one can apply the interior regularity theory for elliptic equations to (2.10) and assert that S^∈C1​(0,L)\hat{S}\in C^{1}(0,L). Clearly, hx​(ϱ0)=0h_{x}(\varrho_{0})=0. Since S^​(ϱ0)=h⁡(ϱ0)=hm​i​n\hat{S}(\varrho_{0})=h(\varrho_{0})=h_{min} and S^≥hm​i​n\hat{S}\geq h_{min} due to (2.12), we infer that S^x​(ϱ0)=0\hat{S}_{x}(\varrho_{0})=0.

On the other hand, by (2.10), S^\hat{S} satisfies

−dS​S^x​x=Λ−S^ in​(ϱ0−ϵ1,ϱ0+ϵ1)∖{ϱ0}.\displaystyle-d_{S}\hat{S}_{xx}=\Lambda-\hat{S}\ \ \ \mbox{ in}\ (\varrho_{0}-\epsilon_{1},\varrho_{0}+\epsilon_{1})\setminus\{\varrho_{0}\}. (3.29)

By using S^x​(ϱ0)=0\hat{S}_{x}(\varrho_{0})=0 and (3.29), one can easily see that S^\hat{S} is increasing in (ϱ0−ϵ1,ϱ0)(\varrho_{0}-\epsilon_{1},\varrho_{0}) while S^\hat{S} is decreasing in (ϱ0,ϱ0+ϵ1)(\varrho_{0},\varrho_{0}+\epsilon_{1}). If (2) happens, without loss of generality, we can find two points, say z1,z2z_{1},\,z_{2} with ϱ0<z1<z2<ϱ0+ϵ2\varrho_{0}<z_{1}<z_{2}<\varrho_{0}+\epsilon_{2} for some small ϵ2>0\epsilon_{2}>0 such that

The above argument shows that (3) must hold. which yields the expression of μ⁡({x})\mu(\{x\}). ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.3.

We first prove (i). We proceed indirectly and suppose that S^≢h\hat{S}\not\equiv h on [0,L][0,L]. {−dSS^x​x=Λ−S^,x∈(ℓ1,ℓ2),S^​(ℓi)=h⁡(ℓi)orS^x​(ℓi)=0,i=1,2.\begin{cases}-d_{S}\hat{S}_{xx}=\Lambda-\hat{S},\ \ \ \ x\in(\ell_{1},\ell_{2}),\vskip 2.84526pt\\ \hat{S}(\ell_{i})=h(\ell_{i})\ \ \mbox{or}\ \ \hat{S}_{x}(\ell_{i})=0,\ \ i=1,2.\end{cases} (3.35)

Hence, (2.15) holds, and (2.16) follows from (2.10) by using a test-function argument similarly as before. Therefore, (i) is proved.

We next prove (ii). First of all, let us consider the case of τ0∈(0,L)\tau_{0}\in(0,L). In this case, the assertions (2.17)-(2.20) follow from Lemma 3.2, and it remains to show that τ1,τ2\tau_{1},\,\tau_{2} are uniquely determined by (2.21). As S^<h\hat{S}<h in [0,τ1)[0,\tau_{1}), we have

Assume that e2LdS−1/2−1e2LdS−1/2+1≤−dS1/2​hx​(L)Λ−h⁡(L)\frac{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}-1}{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}+1}\leq-\frac{d_{S}^{1/2}h_{x}(L)}{\Lambda-h(L)}. We first show that τ1>0\tau_{1}>0 is impossible. On the contrary, we suppose that τ1>0\tau_{1}>0, and by the above analysis, τ1\tau_{1} must solve the first equation of (2.21). Let us consider the following auxiliary problem:

Hence, S^<h\hat{S}<h in [0,L)[0,L) and μ⁡([0,L))=0\mu([0,L))=0, and so S^\hat{S} solves (2.23). It remains to prove (2.24). Indeed, by integrating the sum of (1.6), we obtain

Λ​L−∫0LS⁡(x)​𝑑x=∫0Lη⁡(x)​I​(x)​𝑑x,∀dI>0.\Lambda L-\int_{0}^{L}S(x){\rm d}x=\int_{0}^{L}\eta(x)I(x){\rm d}x,\ \ \forall d_{I}>0.

The case of τ0=0\tau_{0}=0 can be treated similarly as above. In view of Lemma 3.4 and the analysis above, the assertions in (iii) follow immediately. The proof is completed. ∎

4. Discussions and numerical simulations

In recent years, many reaction-diffusion models have been proposed to investigate the transmission dynamics of infectious diseases in a heterogeneous environment. For example, models associated with (1.1) have been studied in [2, 18, 16, 19, 35, 36, 39, 40, 49, 50, 51, 52, 55, 56, 59, 61, 68]. When the random diffusion is not present, such kind of models have been explored in [1, 3, 20, 21, 42, 38, 62, 66, 67] and the references therein. One may also refer to [14, 22, 23, 32, 41, 33, 37, 58, 63, 64, 70, 71] for relevant studies on the effect of random diffusion on the dynamics of infectious diseases.

In this paper, we have investigated the steady state solution (namely, EE) of the SIS epidemic reaction-diffusion models (1.2) and (1.6), in which the disease transmission is governed by the well-known mass action infection mechanism, due to Kermack and McKendrick [26]. In model (1.2), the total population number of the susceptible and infected populations is a constant, while in model (1.6), the total population number is varying, which results from the inclusion of the recruitment for the susceptible population and the death of the infected population. Our purpose is to determine the spatial profile of EE as the movement rate dId_{I} of the infected individuals tends to zero. Such kind of information may be useful for decision-makers to predict the pattern of disease occurrence and henceforth to develop effective disease control strategies.

The previous works [39, 65] derived partial results regarding the spatial profile of EE for (1.2) and (1.6) as dI→0d_{I}\to 0; however, a precise characterization for the distribution of susceptible and infected populations is lacking. In the present work, we have provided a comprehensive understanding on this issue. Below we shall summarize the main theoretical findings of this paper, which will also be supported or complemented by our numerical simulation results.

4.1. Profile of EE of model (1.2) as dI→0d_{I}\to 0.

As pointed out before, when the risk function k⁡(x)=γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)k(x)=\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)} is a constant on the entire habitat [0,L][0,L], then (k,NL−k)(k,\frac{N}{L}-k) is the unique EE of (1.2) provided that k<NLk<\frac{N}{L}, while (NL,0)(\frac{N}{L},0) is the unique disease-free equilibrium of (1.2) provided that k≥NLk\geq\frac{N}{L}. Indeed, in such a trivial case, one can follow the same analysis as in [16, Theorem 4.1] to conclude that (k,NL−k)(k,\frac{N}{L}-k) is a global attractor of (1.1) if k<NLk<\frac{N}{L} and (NL,0)(\frac{N}{L},0) is a global attractor of (1.4) if k≥NLk\geq\frac{N}{L}. Thus, unless otherwise specified, we always assume below that the risk function k⁡(x)=γ⁡(x)β⁡(x)k(x)=\frac{\gamma(x)}{\beta(x)} is non-constant on [0,L][0,L].

According to Theorem 2.1, for model (1.2), one finds that the susceptible population SS converges to the positive constant km​i​nk_{min} as dI→0d_{I}\to 0, which means that the susceptible will always distribute homogeneously on the entire habitat once the movement of the infected individuals is restricted to be sufficiently small. Nevertheless, the profile of the infected population II as dI→0d_{I}\to 0 crucially depends on the distribution behavior of the highest-risk set Θk\Theta_{k} of the risk function k⁡(x)k(x). More precisely, concerning the profile of II for model (1.2), we have the following findings.

(i) If Θk\Theta_{k} consists of a single point, then II must concentrate only at such a highest-risk point.

(ii) If Θk\Theta_{k} contains only multiple isolated points, it follows from Remark 2.1 that II will also concentrate at least at one of those highest-risk points, and the disease will vanish elsewhere. As shown in Figure 1(a)-(b)-(c) for three typical cases, our simulation results suggest that II should concentrate at all such highest-risk points, though the population number of II at each such highest-risk point may vary, depending on the functions β,γ\beta,\,\gamma.

(iii) If Θk\Theta_{k} contains at least one proper interval, then no concentration phenomenon occurs for the disease distribution, and the infected population will aggregate only on such intervals consisting of highest-risk points, regardless of whether there are isolated highest-risk points or not (see Figure 2(a)-(b)). Indeed, our numerical results indicate that the infected population will aggregate on all such intervals consisting of highest-risk points (see Figure 2(c)); however the population number of II at each such interval may be different, depending on the functions β,γ\beta,\,\gamma.

4.2. Profile of EE of model (1.6) as dI→0d_{I}\to 0.

For model (1.6), for the general Hölder continuous risk function hh, under the condition (2.9), as dI→0d_{I}\to 0, we know from Theorem 2.2 that the susceptible population SS converges to a positive function S^\hat{S}, which is non-constant unless hh is constant. The infected population II converges to a positive Radon measure μ\mu, whose support is contained in the region in which S^\hat{S} touches hh; in other words, the disease stays only within the place where the susceptible population distributes along the risk function. If the risk function hh is of C2C^{2}, we see from Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.3 that the infected population aggregates at least in a neighborhood of the highest-risk locations.

Furthermore, when h∈C2​([0,L])h\in C^{2}([0,L]), in light of Theorem 2.3, one can draw the following conclusions concerning the asymptotic profile of II.

(i) For any risk function hh satisfying −dS​hx​x≤Λ−h-d_{S}h_{xx}\leq\Lambda-h in (0,L)(0,L), hx​(0)≥0,hx​(L)≤0h_{x}(0)\geq 0,\,h_{x}(L)\leq 0, and condition (2.9) (for instance, h<Λh<\Lambda is a positive constant), the infected population must occupy the entire habitat, and it also forms the concentration phenomenon at the boundary point x=0x=0 (or x=1x=1) if hx​(0)>0h_{x}(0)>0 (or hx​(1)<0h_{x}(1)<0), which is also the highest-risk location; see Theorem 2.3(i) and the numerical illustrations in Figure 3(a)-(b)-(c).

(ii) For any convex risk function hh (i.e., hx​x≥,≢0h_{xx}\geq,\not\equiv 0 on [0,L][0,L]) fulfilling (2.9), the infected population usually stays only in part of the habitat. In particular, by Theorem 2.3(ii)(iii), we can observe the following behaviors.

(ii-a) If the highest-risk set Θh\Theta_{h} contains only one point, denoted by τ0\tau_{0}, then the distribution behavior of the infected population is affected by whether τ0\tau_{0} is a boundary point or an interior point. More precisely, when τ0\tau_{0} is an interior point, then the infected population resides in a certain left neighborhood of τ0\tau_{0}, staying away from the boundary points x=0x=0 and x=1x=1. In fact, such a neighborhood can be calculated through the formula (2.21). One may further refer to Figure 4(a).

However, if τ0\tau_{0} is a boundary point, say τ0=L\tau_{0}=L, then the infected population stays in a certain neighborhood of LL provided e2LdS−1/2−1e2LdS−1/2+1>−dS1/2​hx​(L)Λ−h⁡(L)\frac{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}-1}{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}+1}>-\frac{d_{S}^{1/2}h_{x}(L)}{\Lambda-h(L)}, while the infected population concentrates only at LL provided e2LdS−1/2−1e2LdS−1/2+1≤−dS1/2​hx​(L)Λ−h⁡(L)\frac{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}-1}{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}+1}\leq-\frac{d_{S}^{1/2}h_{x}(L)}{\Lambda-h(L)}. Since hx​(L)≤0h_{x}(L)\leq 0 in this situation, the infected population stays in a certain neighborhood of LL provided for all dS>0d_{S}>0 if hx​(L)=0h_{x}(L)=0. If hx​(L)<0h_{x}(L)<0, it should be noted that the function q(dS)=dS−1/2e2LdS−1/2−1e2LdS−1/2+1+hx​(L)Λ−h⁡(L)q(d_{S})=d_{S}^{-1/2}\frac{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}-1}{e^{2Ld_{S}^{-1/2}}+1}+\frac{h_{x}(L)}{\Lambda-h(L)} deceases in dS∈(0,∞)d_{S}\in(0,\infty), limdS→0q⁡(dS)=∞\lim_{d_{S}\to 0}q(d_{S})=\infty and limdS→∞q⁡(dS)=hx​(L)Λ−h⁡(L)<0\lim_{d_{S}\to\infty}q(d_{S})=\frac{h_{x}(L)}{\Lambda-h(L)}<0. As a result, there is a unique dS∗>0d_{S}^{*}>0 such that q⁡(dS∗)=0q(d_{S}^{*})=0, and in turn the infected population stays in a left neighborhood of LL for 0<dS<dS∗0<d_{S}<d_{S}^{*} , and the infected population concentrates only at LL for all dS≥dS∗d_{S}\geq d_{S}^{*}.

(ii-b) If the highest-risk set Θh\Theta_{h} contains only an interval, then the infected population resides in a certain neighborhood of such an interval. Again, such a neighborhood can be calculated through the formula (2.21). See the numerical simulation in Figure 4(b).

(ii-c) For a general Hölder continuous risk function hh, we can conclude that the disease must exist in all isolated highest-risk point(s) and a neighborhood of each highest-risk interval if exists; nevertheless, it is challenging to give a precise characterization for the distribution behavior of the susceptible and infected populations, due to the mathematical difficulties on the analysis of the free boundary problem (2.10). We have performed the numerical simulations in Figure 5(a)-(b) as an illustration.

In what follows, we would like to make some more discussions on (ii-a) above in the case that τ0\tau_{0} is a boundary point. For example, we take τ0=L\tau_{0}=L, and also assume that hx​(L)<0h_{x}(L)<0. On the one hand, by fixing hx​(L)h_{x}(L), we have known from (ii-b) that large diffusion rate dSd_{S} can result in the disease concentration only at the location LL and small diffusion rate dSd_{S} will cause the disease to distribute in a left neighborhood of LL. On the other hand, once dSd_{S} is fixed, the concentration phenomenon happens only if −hx​(L)-h_{x}(L) is properly large. This motivates us to see whether a similar concentration phenomenon could occur at an interior isolated highest-risk point if the risk function hh is merely Hölder continuous. To illustrate this phenomenon, let us consider the following risk function whose curve is the connection of two segments:

h⁡(x)={a1​(x−L2)+Λ4,x∈[0,L2],a2​(x−L2)+Λ4,x∈(L2,L],h(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}a_{1}\left(x-\frac{L}{2}\right)+\frac{\Lambda}{4},&x\in\left[0,\frac{L}{2}\right],\\[5.69054pt] a_{2}\left(x-\frac{L}{2}\right)+\frac{\Lambda}{4},&x\in\left(\frac{L}{2},L\right],\end{array}\right. (4.1)

with a1​<0,a2>​0a_{1}<0,a_{2}>0. Obviously, hh is merely Lipschitz continuous at x=L2x=\frac{L}{2}. Our numerical simulation results demonstrate that if the slopes |a1|,a2|a_{1}|,\,a_{2} are properly large, then the infected population will concentrate at x=L2x=\frac{L}{2} (Figure 6(a)); if |a1|,a2|a_{1}|,\,a_{2} are small, then the infected population will aggregate in a neighborhood of x=L2x=\frac{L}{2} (Figure 6(b)); and if |a1||a_{1}| is small while a2a_{2} is large, then the infected population will aggregate in a left-neighborhood of x=L2x=\frac{L}{2} (Figure 6(b)). These profiles behave rather differently from that in Theorem 2.3(ii) for h∈C2​([0,L])h\in C^{2}([0,L]), as shown by Figure 4(a). Therefore, the numerical results reveal that the smoothness of hh may have a substantial effect on the spatial distribution of the disease.

4.3. Conclusion.

The discussions in the above two subsections, together with the numerical simulations, show that the spatial profile of the susceptible and infected populations of (1.2) and (1.6) with respect to small movement rate of the infected individuals are rather different. This is caused by the presence of the recruitment term for the susceptible population and the death rate for the infected population. On the other hand, we would like to mention that the recent works [11, 12, 13, 14, 31, 34, 69] studied various kinds of reaction-diffusion-advection SIS epidemic models, in which the advection term represents some passive movement in a certain direction, e.g., due to external environmental forces such as water flow [46, 47, 48, 57], wind [15] and so on. In particular, if an advection is present in (1.2) and stands for, for instance, the water flow, it was proved in [13, Theorem 1.4] that, as dI→0d_{I}\to 0, the susceptible population converges to a positive function while the infected population concentrates only at the downstream of the water flow; a similar result can be shown to hold for the corresponding system (1.6). Such a distribution behavior is essentially different from that of (1.2) and (1.6) with small dId_{I}.

In summary, our results here, combined with those of [13, 31, 40], suggest that the recruitment term for the susceptible population, the death rate for the infected population (even the smoothness of the associated risk function) as well as the advection can lead to significant impacts on the disease transmission and thus decision-makers should attach great importance to these factors when taking measures such as the lockdown and quarantine to control the movement or immigration of the infected individuals so as to eliminate the disease infection.
